1	# Task 11: Solar-system explorer with focus on click
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite, rendering to the canvas with id #app. The app is an interactive, stylised solar system explorer on a dark starfield background.
4	
5	Show a glowing central star and at least 6 planets, each at a different orbital distance, with a different size and colour and orbiting the star at a different speed (inner planets faster). At least one planet has a moon orbiting it, and at least one planet has a ring. Draw a thin circular orbit line for each planet. Planets should also spin about their own axis. Use a simple procedural look (colour, gradients or generated textures); do not load external assets from the network.
6	
7	The user can click a planet to focus on it. On focus, the camera smoothly moves (about 1.5 seconds, eased) to a close view of that planet and keeps following it as it orbits, and a DOM info panel appears showing the planet's name, its orbital period in Earth days, and its distance from the star in million km. Clicking empty space, or pressing the Escape key, smoothly returns to the overview showing the whole system and hides the panel. In the overview, the user can drag to orbit the camera around the system and scroll to zoom within sensible limits. Add a toggle button labelled 'Pause' that stops and resumes orbital motion, and shows 'Play' while paused.
8	
9	The scene must look correct on first load with no console errors. Expose

1	# three.js asset bridge (`aura3d import-three`)
2	
3	Carry procedural three.js content into an Aura3D project as a typed asset plus editable Aura3D source, instead of
4	porting it by hand. The bridge carries assets, animation clips, simple shaders, lights, camera and renderer output.
5	Behaviour (input, physics, scoring, UI) stays native Aura3D code. It is a build-time tool: `three` is a dev
6	dependency of your project, never a runtime dependency, and the shipped route imports only `@aura3d/engine`.
7	
8	Status: prototype (B1). Every run writes a report of what was carried, approximated or left out; read it before
9	you show the result.
10	
11	## When to use it
12	
13	| You have | Use |
14	| --- | --- |
15	| A three.js function that builds a scene from code (procedural props, a generated city, an animated rig, a shader showcase) | `aura3d import-three` |

Setting setPose each frame should override the rig's own update, though there's likely a one-frame lag between the planet's motion and the camera following it—probably acceptable given the small delta.

For the camera setup, I'm calculating the distance and elevation needed so the full orbit radius of the outermost planet fits comfortably within the field of view at a 16:9 aspect ratio.

I'm defining each planet's size and the sun's radius, then setting up lighting with a point light at the center, ambient fill, an emissive sun material, and a bloom effect for glow. Now I'm thinking through how the three.js export will name the objects dynamically.

content.thinking:
The GLB asset setup looks good, so now I'm planning the main scene file: setting up the background color, adding the backdrop model, configuring neutral environment lighting, and adding a point light for illumination.

For the sun, I'm thinking a scaled unit sphere with emissive material or a solar shader, testing to find the right size and intensity. For planets, I'll generate textures procedurally via canvas gradients and band/noise patterns tailored per planet, apply spin rotation, and probably skip axial tilt for simplicity.

Saturn's rings need custom annulus geometry with radial UV mapping and an alpha canvas texture for the banding, using a double-sided blended material. I'll add one moon for Earth orbiting at a small radius, skip Jupiter's moons, and draw orbit paths as simple unlit line loops in a muted blue-gray color.

For the camera, I'm designing a state machine: an overview mode using spherical coordinates (yaw, pitch, distance) controlled by drag and scroll with clamped zoom range, and a focus mode where the camera targets a planet and positions itself offset by a distance scaled to the planet's radius (larger for Saturn to account for its rings), choosing an angle that keeps the lit side visible rather than putting the planet's dark side toward the camera.

I'm refining this offset to blend radial and tangential components with some vertical elevation so the camera sees a gibbous, mostly-lit view as it tracks the planet's orbital rotation, while checking edge cases like Mercury's close view distance to make sure the camera doesn't end up uncomfortably close to or inside the sun's radius.

For transitions, I'm planning smooth eased interpolation from the current pose to a recomputed goal pose over about 1.5 seconds, with unfocusing reverting to the user's previous overview orbit parameters.

Orbit dragging should only apply in overview mode, and I'm considering whether wheel zoom should adjust focus distance while focused, tracking camera distance relative to whichever planet is targeted.

For input handling, I'm distinguishing clicks from drags by pointer movement threshold, then picking planets by projecting them to screen space and testing hit radius with nearest-depth priority -- handling focus, refocus, and unfocus cases depending on what's clicked. Now I'm working out the projection math using camera position, target, up vector, and field of view.

I need to use the actual presented camera pose for picking to avoid a frame of lag, bind pointer events natively on the canvas with pointer capture, and make the wheel listener non-passive so I can preventDefault.

For the panel overlay, I need to check index.html to see where the 640x360 canvas sits in the page, since the pause button is also DOM-based.
